I've written the letter, but I didn't make it say you're the main reason the scores went up. Your GM watched the lobby and every room get renovated during those same 18 months. If the letter credits you alone for the score, they'll know it can't be proven, and they may start doubting your other numbers too. Instead, the letter points out that the check-in score is about the front desk, and that the desk's results are things you can prove (training, retention). That makes the claim stronger, not weaker.

I also brought up the budget gap myself. Your GM already knows about it, and naming it first with a plan reads as manager-level thinking. If you've done any scheduling or labor-hour work during these 7 weeks, add it there, because payroll is mostly scheduling.

Fill in the bracketed parts before sending.

<final_document>
To: [GM name]
From: [Your name], Assistant Front Office Manager
Date: [Date]
Re: Application for Front Office Manager

I'm applying for the Front Office Manager position. I've worked at this hotel for six years, the last two as Assistant Front Office Manager, and for the past seven weeks I've run the front office on my own. Here is what I've done and what I'll bring to the role.

**I've already been doing the job.**
Since [previous FOM's name] left seven weeks ago, I've covered every part of the front office manager's role by myself, including [scheduling, staffing, guest escalations, reporting: list what applies]. The desk has kept running without a gap in leadership.

**I built a team that stays.**
In the year before I became assistant manager, 9 of our 14 front desk employees left. Last year, 5 of 14 left. That's a drop from 64% turnover to 36%. Every person we keep saves us the cost of hiring and training a replacement, and it means guests are checked in by experienced staff.

**I rewrote how we train.**
I rebuilt the front desk training program. New hires used to need 9 shifts before they could work the desk alone. Now they need 5. That's almost half the training time per hire, and new staff become productive sooner.

**Check-in scores rose while I was focused on the desk.**
Over the last 18 months, our check-in score on [review site] went from 7.9 to 8.6. The renovation gave guests a better lobby and better rooms, and that helped. But the check-in score measures the moment guests spend with our front desk staff, and those staff were better trained and more experienced than before. I'm proud of my team's part in that number.

**Where I still need to grow: budget.**
I haven't owned a budget yet, and I know this role is responsible for a $1.1 million payroll. My plan for the first 90 days:
- Meet with you and [controller/finance contact] to learn how the payroll budget is built and tracked
- Review the last two years of front office labor costs against occupancy
- [Complete a hotel finance course, e.g., through AHLEI or eCornell]
- Give you a monthly labor-cost report so you can see my progress

I know this hotel, this team, and this job. I'd like the chance to keep doing it as Front Office Manager.

[Your name]
</final_document>

If you know the turnover numbers for the previous FOM's years, or any guest comments that mention desk staff by name, they'd make the case even stronger. Send them over and I'll add them.
